Bangor.wildlife_intro:
Bangor is the urban center of northern and eastern Maine, and its wildlife calls have an urban weight the smaller towns do not see. Norway rats persist in older downtown and riverfront buildings, raccoons and gray squirrels work the mature trees of the Broadway historic district and the Great Fire district onto aging rooflines, and bats colonize the attics of the city's many large historic homes each summer. The Penobscot River and the Kenduskeag Stream valley pull raccoons, skunks and beavers through the city, and the City Forest puts deep woods against suburban backyards.

Older, larger homes mean multi-entry jobs — our crew expects to find several gaps on a historic Bangor roofline and seals all of them in one complete job. Commercial and rental properties need the same thoroughness, plus the documentation landlords and buyers ask for. Bat work is exclusion only, under Maine timing rules. Call us for homes, rentals and downtown buildings alike; Bangor's housing rewards owners who fix the whole envelope, not just the loudest hole.

Millinocket.wildlife_intro:
Millinocket sits at the edge of the biggest forest in the eastern United States, and its wildlife calls reflect that address. In town, the well-built mill-era homes still draw bats to their attics, raccoons to their chimneys and gray squirrels to their rooflines, while the former mill structures shelter pigeons, bats and raccoons at scale. Out on Millinocket Lake and the Baxter road, camps face the woods directly: porcupines chewing all winter, red squirrels in the eaves, beavers flooding camp roads, and fishers in the deep woods behind the camps.

As the mill era recedes, many Millinocket homes and camps change hands or sit quieter than they used to — exactly the conditions animals exploit. Our crew seals camps and homes completely, armors porcupine targets, and plans bat exclusions around Maine law, including the June and July bar on unoccupied buildings. Moose and bear here belong to the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife; the building problems belong to us. Call us before winter closing or at spring opening.

Orono.wildlife_intro:
Orono's wildlife calls run on the academic calendar. Student rentals and converted older homes near the University of Maine sit lightly occupied over breaks and summers, and gray squirrels, raccoons and bats claim the quiet attics — landlords meet the damage at turnover. The Stillwater River cuts through town with raccoons and skunks along its banks, family neighborhoods see the standard attic and chimney work, and the Pushaw Lake road adds camps with porcupine and beaver problems.

Turnover housing needs a different discipline: inspect at every vacancy, seal completely in durable materials, and document the building's condition. Our crew does exactly that for Orono landlords and homeowners, and times bat exclusions to Maine rules so a summer vacancy does not become a legal problem. Squirrels here are persistent and excellent climbers; half-measures fail predictably. Call us at the first vacancy or the first noise — in a college town, the cheapest wildlife job is the one done before the next lease starts.
